I did not try this example.  But tried a simple one:

parameters {
    real y[1];
}

model {
    y[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
}


In RStan, if we set_cppo('debug'), R would not crash for this example.  set_cppo('debug') would not set -DNDEBUG flag. By default, Stan does not set this flag.  If -DNDEBUG is set in Stan, Stan will exit with a segfault for this example.  

When set_cppo('debug') is set in RStan, for this example, R would not crash. 

> set_cppo('debug')

+ parameters {
+ real y[1];
+ }
+ 

+ model {
+ y[2] ~ normal(0, 1);
+ }
+ '

> library(rstan)

I'm afraid we need to keep the range checks in place
all the time by default. Otherwise, there's no way to
stop segfaults from taking down R or the command.

Stan is not like JAGS or BUGS where the loops are all
determined when the data is read in. In Stan, loops can
have bounds that depend on random quantities being sampled:

for (n in 1:floor(Z)) { ... }

I'm OK with a power-user mode that turns all the checking
off. I think that'll be easier to write and understand,

On 10/27/12 10:12 PM, Ben Goodrich wrote:
> Perhaps another question is why does it segfault for some compiler options and throw an exception for others?

Stan array indexing is std::vector indexing
with operator[](), not with at().

Turns out that in g++, you can enable exception throwing
for out-of-range std::vector operator[]() indexing with
_GLIBCXX_DEBUG.

Otherwise, you get a bad memory write, the behavior
of which isn't specified (i.e., it can vary wildly
by platform, compiler config, or even from run to run
depending on where the program's loaded into memory).

gdb itself will run the code differently, so error
behavior from out-of-range writing can differ there
from its behavior "in the wild".

C++ is perhaps a little too close to the road
to my own taste.

- Bob
